text: Name a historic AI program or system
note: Built before the year 2000: programs, expert systems, game players, chatbots, robots and machines

aka: Machine Educable Noughts And Crosses Engine
answers.q: 304 matchboxes full of coloured beads that learned noughts and crosses. Donald Michie's 1961 RL.
Claude Shannon's 1950 maze-solving mechanical mouse. The original Claude in AI.
In 1999 it flew NASA's Deep Space 1 on its own for a couple of days.
Dickmanns's Mercedes drove itself on Paris motorways in 1994.
Answered geologists' questions about Apollo moon rocks in 1971.
David Cope's composer program. Its fake Bach fooled audiences.
Bell Labs, 1952: recognized spoken digits, if you were the right speaker.
Ken Thompson's chess machine. The US government briefly seized it as a munition.
Soviet program, first world computer chess champion in 1974.
Turing's 1948 chess algorithm. No computer could run it, so he executed it by hand.
Torres Quevedo's 1912 automaton played a king-and-rook endgame for real.
Creative Labs' 1991 sound-card therapist. PLEASE ENTER YOUR NAME.
Michael Mauldin's 1990s TinyMUD bot. He coined the word 'chatterbot' for it.
1996 game whose Norns had neural-net brains and simulated biochemistry.
Richard Wallace's AIML chatbot, 1995. Three-time Loebner Prize winner.
CMU chess machine named after the Hitchhiker's computer. The team moved to IBM and built Deep Blue.
1954: 60-odd Russian sentences into English, and a promise that MT would be solved in 3 to 5 years.
Harold Cohen's painting program, started around 1973 and refined for four decades.
It looks like you're writing a letter. Built on Bayesian models from Microsoft Research's Lumière project.
Minsky's 1951 vacuum-tube neural net, partly built from a B-24 autopilot.
Credited author of 'The Policeman's Beard Is Half Constructed' (1984).
Lenat's program won the Traveller naval wargame title in 1981 with a weird fleet, then again in 1982.
Selfridge's 1959 model of 'demons' shrieking at each other to recognize patterns.
Beat Othello world champion Takeshi Murakami 6–0 in 1997.
Two late-1940s vacuum-tube robots that found their way home to the charger.
Stanford's blood-infection expert system. Matched specialists in tests, never used on real patients.
1965, Stanford: inferred molecular structure from mass spectra. Usually called the first expert system.
SRI's 1960s robot. Gave the world A* and STRIPS along the way.
Tesauro's 1992 self-play backgammon net. Human experts changed their opening moves because of it.
Arthur Samuel's checkers player, the program behind the phrase 'machine learning' (1959).
Read a big share of US bank cheques in the late '90s.
Checkers world champion in 1994. In 2007 its team solved checkers outright: perfect play is a draw.
Fukushima, 1980: convolution and pooling a decade before LeNet.
Lenat started hand-coding common sense in 1984. Still going.
DEC's R1 configured VAX orders and saved millions a year. The expert-system boom's poster child.

aka: Autonomous Land Vehicle in a Neural Network
answers.q: 1989: a tiny neural net that steered CMU's Navlab straight from camera pixels.
Sejnowski and Rosenberg's net learned to read aloud, babbling like a baby along the way.
Colby's paranoid patient, 1972. It once had a therapy session with ELIZA over the ARPANET.
Moved blocks on command in 1970. Named after ETAOIN SHRDLU, the order of keys on a Linotype.
1956. Proved 38 of Principia's first 52 theorems, one more neatly than Russell and Whitehead.
Weizenbaum's 1966 fake therapist. His secretary asked him to leave the room so she could keep chatting.
Beat Kasparov in 1997. IBM retired it right after, no rematch.
1958 NYT: the Navy expects it to 'walk, talk, see, write, reproduce itself'. Still waiting.
